subjects.displayTitle: Muhammad and Islam: recognition beyond inherited prejudice
subjects.introduction: For more than a thousand years, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observed, Christians and Muslims have regarded each other through a fog of misunderstanding, and He insisted that the fog was not the fault of either faith but of imitation and inherited prejudice. Clearing it begins with a simple act: read the Qur’án for yourself, as Bahá’u’lláh urges, and let the tradition speak before its critics do. What then comes into view is a Prophet of mercy who appeared in a desert empty of learning and kings, suffered thirteen years of persecution, protected the Christians of Najrán, and drew warring tribes into a single fellowship from which schools, sciences and a civilisation flowed as far as Europe. Bahá’ís call themselves people of the Qur’án and would bear witness to Muhammad under the sword. The Qur’án’s own description of His mission as a mercy to the peoples [1] sets the measure for everything else: the hardship borne with patience, the transformation of conduct, the argument from changed lives rather than demanded marvels. Reverent, unbiased study is where the journey settles, and from there it opens onto the interpretation of Qur’án and Hadith, the meaning of the Seal of the Prophets, and the early history of Islam and the family of Muhammad, where recognition and rejection first took shape.
subjects.arc: Begin with reconciliation and mercy, consider the grounds of recognition, and move through history and devotion toward informed study.

order.why: Invite direct reading of the Qur’an.
shortened: Say: Perused ye not the Qur'an? Read it, that haply ye may find the Truth, for this Book is verily the Straight Path. This is the Way of God unto all who are in the heavens and all who are on the earth.

order.why: Open with the possibility of overcoming inherited religious hostility.
Center the image of a Prophet of mercy.
Read the explicit profession of faith grounded in investigation.
shortened: Convey my respectful greetings to Shukri Effendi and say: We are people of the Qur'an, we are believers in the Messenger of God, peace be upon Him. We are firm in the Covenant and Testament, and in this path we sacrifice our lives. We believe in all the Prophets, making no distinction between any of His Messengers. For our faith is real, not metaphorical; it is based on investigation, not blind imitation.

order.why: Retain the concise affirmation of the truth of Islam.
Consider the effort to correct a public misunderstanding.
Read recognition voiced within other religious settings.
Hear the reported encounter with Christian missionaries.
Examine the proposal to judge a religious educator through demonstrated effects.
Connect education with reconciliation among divided peoples.
shortened: It is therefore evident that mankind requires a universal divine educator who can gather the diverse peoples under the shadow of one Word, cause contending nations to drink from a single fountain, transform enmity and hatred into love and fellowship, and convert strife and conflict into peace and tranquility. Thus did the Prophet Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon Him) unite the warring, hostile, and savage tribes of the Arabian desert and bring them together under the pavilion of unity. As a result, those desert Arabs achieved tremendous progress, raised the banner of perfection in both spiritual and material realms, and attained everlasting glory.

order.why: Read fraternity as a fruit of spiritual education.
shortened: Muhammad appeared as a Prophet among such a people. He educated these barbarous tribes, lifted them out of their ignorance and savagery and put an end to the continuous strife and hatred which had existed among them. He established agreement and reconciliation among them, unified them and taught them to look upon each other as brothers. Through His training they advanced rapidly in prestige and civilization.

order.why: Consider the reported account of changed conduct and belief in earlier prophets.
Read the argument from civilization while attending to its historical rhetoric.
shortened: The Arabs then excelled all the peoples of the world in science and the arts, in industry and invention, in philosophy, government and moral character. And truly, the rise of this brutish and despicable element, in such a short interval, to the supreme heights of human perfection, is the greatest demonstration of the rightfulness of the Lord Muhammad's Prophethood.

order.why: Keep the account of learning and cultural transmission in its source setting.
shortened: When the Beauty of Muhammad dawned from the horizon of Yathrib and Bat'ha, the religion of God manifested such power and might that in a brief span these ignorant peoples became the foremost among the learned in all sciences and arts, and perfected the deficiencies in the sciences and arts of the philosophers. Likewise, in all degrees of progress they reached the highest pinnacle, such that Baghdad became the center of learning and Bukhara the source of the arts, and knowledge raised such a standard in Andalusia that all the learned ones of Europe came to the schools of Cordova and Cordoba to acquire the light of knowledge from the lamp of Islamic schools.

order.why: Consider persecution, protection, and learning together.
shortened: For thirteen years He suffered at their hands every conceivable tribulation, till at last He fled the city and emigrated to Medina. And yet, far from desisting, these people joined forces, raised an army, and attacked with the aim of exterminating every man, woman, and child among His followers.

Muhammad never fought against the Christians; on the contrary, He treated them with consideration and accorded them complete freedom. In Najran there lived a community of Christians, and they were under His care and protection. Muhammad said: "Should anyone infringe upon their rights, I myself will be his enemy and will charge him before God."

order.why: Read the transformation of oppressed peoples as the passage’s evidence of a mission.
Consider the extension of a civilization through its teaching.
shortened: Mohammed through his power was enabled to elevate a nation, for on his teachings a mighty civilization was constructed in the Arabian peninsula, the influence of which, as recorded in history, extended as far west as Spain.

order.why: Read the stated connection with European learning as an attributed historical argument.
Retain the related reported account of schools and the spread of knowledge.
Connect the image of light with justice and education.
Consider the formation of virtues as an inward measure of change.
Hear the reported questions about the power of spiritual transformation.
shortened: How was it that when His Holiness Mohamed appeared in that great chersonese or Arabian peninsula, a mighty spiritual revolution shook that empire-desert to its centre? With what power did the Prophet of Allah change the character of the primitive, savage Arabs, reformed their social customs, unified the heterogeneous, independent nomadic tribes and created in their midst a spiritual democracy? With what Light did he illumine the waste Sahara?

order.why: Read the description of the mission’s setting without treating its rhetoric as an account of a people today.
shortened: As for the Holy Apostle Muhammad, the one chosen by God (Peace be upon him), God raised him up in a valley without farms, where nothing would grow, among a discordant multitude of warlike peoples, among tribes who had fallen to the depths of ignorance and blindness, not knowing who spread out the earth, not recognizing a single character in the Book, not understanding any part of God's message. They were scattered in the deserts of Arabia and dwelling in sandy wastelands, subsisting on camel milk, with a few dates and grapes.

order.why: Keep the account of changed customs within its historical argument.
Read the reported contrast between an unlettered educator and the effects of His teaching.
Retain the related reported account with its original attribution.
Ask what new effects a commemoration should recall.
shortened: In any case, tonight is the night of the birth of the Prophet. The Muslims are celebrating His birth, and their celebration consists of thousand-year-old customs which they carry out according to their traditions, rules and practices. But in truth, this birth produced new effects in the world and beneficial results were obtained. This birth caused the condition of Asia to change and transform, moving from one state to another.

order.why: Read the transformation of a place into a center of pilgrimage.
shortened: In any case, I hope they will awaken and become conscious, and at least realize that Muhammad appeared in Mecca when it was but a rocky tract - no trees, no vegetation, no greenery, no meadow, no agriculture, no industry - the dwelling place of savage Arab tribes. When Muhammad appeared from Mecca, Mecca became the Qiblih of Asia, Africa, and some regions of Europe, where all turn to pray, and this rocky tract became the annual center of the greatest gathering of men from Asia and Africa.

order.why: Keep the reported geographic and historical descriptions attributed.
shortened: Consider how the Arabian desert, a wilderness of sand, dried mountains, hot climate, uncultivable ground, savage, primitive inhabitants, the country situated near the Equator - through the appearance of Mohammad and his disciples - became the mother of all the countries, the Kaaba for millions of souls and the object of veneration by all mankind.

order.why: Examine the reported criticism of inconsistent judgments about civilization and intervention.
Read the account of war as a reported historical justification, not a present instruction.
shortened: At the time of Muhammad, He sanctioned war for the preservation of the lives of His followers. The laws of individual justice were confused and preliminary in the souls of men. Therefore, the law of general justice of the community was revealed by this Prophet. He commanded His followers to carry the Religion of God by the sword.

There must be a law to prevent the wolves , from destroying the lambs at such a period of religious history. That is why the Shepherd sanctioned such vigorous protection for the sheep. Behind such laws of a Manifestation there is always a supreme wisdom.

order.why: Retain the distinct prayerful language of conquest.
Read the supplied chronology as the source presents it.
Keep the brief reported travel claim in its setting.
shortened: His Holiness Muhammad came here also. He came here twice, once when he was eleven years old and once when he was twenty-eight.

order.why: Read bereavement and hostile response without silently reconciling the supplied chronology.
shortened: Reflect upon the Seal of the Prophets - may the spirit of all else be sacrificed for His sake. He had five male children who ascended, whereupon the idolaters began to gloat. And when He remained without issue, they called Him - God forbid - "abtar" (cut off).

order.why: Consider persecution and emigration in a devotional account.
shortened: And blessings and peace be upon him whose light shone forth from the horizon of Batha, and through whose appearance the regions were adorned, and the herald proclaimed: "O people of the earth! He Who was promised hath come, and through Him have appeared the most excellent names of God and His most exalted attributes" - he against whom the idolaters arose until the decree of emigration came from God, the Lord of all beings.

order.why: Join mercy with patience under adversity.
Distinguish outward companionship from conduct faithful to the teachings.
Read the request for writing materials within its particular account of succession.
shortened: For in the Sahih of Bukhari---that book of traditions which the people of Sunni Islam account among their sound and authoritative collections, whose transmitters are deemed trustworthy and whose authenticity is held to be above suspicion---it is recorded and set down that when the signs of ascension began to appear upon the blessed countenance of the Messenger of God---may the spirit of all worlds be a sacrifice unto Him---that is, when His radiant face grew flushed, He said: "Bring paper and pen, that I may write and declare something whereby ye shall not go astray after Me, and which ye may follow as your rule of conduct."

order.why: Treat the reported judgment on historical writing as a source’s assessment.
Keep the reported twenty-three years with its original wording and context.
Preserve the supplied reported connection with Sufi natural philosophy.
Read the concise reported statement about religious background and love of humanity.
Keep the reported comparison of spiritual conditions distinct from a universal ranking of religions.
Read the reported image of Rumi’s poetry sustaining a dispensation.
Consider the scriptural refusal to rest recognition on demanded marvels.
Read the related account of miraculous demands and the messenger’s reply.
shortened: In the Quran it is mentioned that seven tribes came before the Secret of Being and Essence of Purpose, His Holiness Muhammad, peace be upon Him. Each made his faith contingent upon a miracle. One said: "Bring down a book from heaven." Another said: "Cast down a fragment of heaven to earth." Another said: "Make a spring to flow." Another said: "Ascend to heaven." Another said: "Show us the Lord with His hosts." Another said: "Produce a treasure." Another said: "Bring forth the lofty paradise." In reply to all of these He declares: "Say: Glory be to my Lord! Am I aught but a mortal messenger?"...

order.why: Hear the Qur’anic appeal to belief and good deeds across communities.
Read the Bab’s appeal to the Qur’an within His claim to revelation.
Consider continuity through the language of prior recognition.
Read finality and promised revelation within this Baha’i interpretation.
Retain the brief statement of glad tidings.
shortened: This is the Day which the Seal of the Prophets--may the life of all else be sacrificed for His sake--gave unto all as a glad-tiding.

order.why: Pause with the invitation to reflect on the Prophet’s days.
shortened: O Muhammad! Reflect upon the days of the Seal of the Prophets - may the spirit of all else but Him be sacrificed for His sake.

order.why: Place humility beside the language of supreme glory.
Read the confession of servanthood and chosen responsibility.
shortened: Thou art God, there is no God but Thee, alone with no partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad - Thy blessings be upon him and his family - is Thy servant whom Thou didst bring into being and choose for Thyself, singling him out for Thy Cause and accepting him for Thy knowledge.

order.why: Consider divine choice and the limits of vision.
Read the testimony offered from the mountain.
shortened: And I bear witness in this my station upon the surface of this mountain that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger, whom He hath chosen from the midst of the apex of creation through the manifestation of His sovereignty, and whom He hath clothed with the garment of grace for the revelation of His grandeur, and made him unique among all peers and equals in the kingdoms of His earth and heaven, that those who seek proofs might know His attributes through His attributes and His qualities through His qualities.

order.why: Hear the concise affirmation of a messenger to the worlds.
Read the prayer’s language of unique honor within its devotional setting.
shortened: Thou didst create Muhammad - Thy blessings be upon him - by Thy command, and didst choose him for Thy covenant, and didst select him for Thy remembrance, and didst single him out for Thy providence, and didst place him above all Thy Prophets and Messengers, and didst establish him upon the station of the sovereignty of Thy oneness in the kingdom of Thy earth and the heaven of Thy lordship, that he might convey unto all things that Thou art God, that there is no God but Thee, and that all else besides Thee is Thy creation and within Thy grasp.

Therefore, O God, send blessings upon Muhammad superior to what Thou hast bestowed upon any of Thy creation, and upon him what Thou hast specially conferred upon any of Thy servants, and more exalted than what Thou hast graciously bestowed upon any of Thy chosen ones, and more glorious than what Thou hast honored any of Thy sincere ones - blessings that have no equal in Thy knowledge, no likeness in Thy Book, no peer in Thy kingdom, and no companion among the manifestations of Thy creation.

order.why: Keep the related affirmation of uniqueness in the source’s voice.
Connect divine unity with law and detachment.
Read the Qur’an as the expression of this mission.
Consider the layered symbolic names bestowed upon Muhammad.
shortened: And blessings and peace be upon the Primal Point, and the upright and curved Alif, and the All-Embracing Word of Power, and the Divine Spirit of the Kingdom, through Whom existence began and the manifestations of the Unseen in the visible world were sealed - Muhammad, the Chosen One, whom God made the Dawning-Place of His most excellent names and the Manifestation of His most exalted attributes - and upon His family and companions from this day until the Day whereon the tongue of might and power shall speak forth [that "the Kingdom on that Day shall be] God's, the One, the All-Compelling."

order.why: Describes the advent of Muhammad as the Resurrection of the preceding dispensation.
Read the title Seal of the Prophets alongside the image of universal guidance.
shortened: Through a single word He created the world and guided it, and appointed the best of creation as Guide, adorning Him with the robe of "Blessed be God, the best of creators" and crowning Him with "Verily He is the Seal of the Prophets." He is the all-embracing Word and He is the Guide of all.

order.why: Retain the devotional account of signs and unity.
Consider knowledge and continuing life through the imagery of revelation.
Follow the image of a barren valley becoming a source of grace.
shortened: This nobility was attained and made manifest through the Muhammadan Revelation and the Ahmadan Light. His grace caused dust to ascend above the heavens, and His mercy enabled the people of the earthly realm of creation to reach the highest Paradise. From the parched valley flowed the Euphrates of grace, and from the veiled Hijaz appeared the Morn of Revelation. Can any likeness be seen for this power, or any similitude be observed? Nay, by His very Self, the Truth! The place that was the abode of idols became the seat of the remembrance of the Lord of all beings.

order.why: Read creation’s testimony and the House as a refuge.
Keep the praise of the Prophet, family, and companions together.
Consider commandments and knowledge as adornments of common life.
shortened: And prayers and peace be upon him through whom Yathrib was honored and the Hijaz smiled - verily he is the Lord through whom God's power was manifested throughout the lands and among the servants - and upon his family and companions who aided the Faith, holding fast to God's mighty cord, and through them the text of the world was adorned with the beauty of commandments and laws, and the faces of nations with the light of His knowledge in the beginning and the end.

order.why: Read the companions through their service to guidance.
Hear the opening of the door of knowledge.
Gather the themes of revelation, knowledge, and law.
shortened: He Who raised Him up and sent Him forth with the truth is verily the Lamp of Guidance amongst mankind, the Sign of the Ancient of Days amidst the nations, the Dawning-Place of His most beautiful names and the Dayspring of His most exalted attributes--He Who was named Muhammad in the kingdom of creation. God made Him the Source of His Revelation, the Repository of His Knowledge, and the Manifestation of His Laws.

order.why: Read the blessing through its varied images of life and light.
Turn praise toward what benefits life in this world and the next.
shortened: I beseech Thee by the Beloved (Muhammad) - concerning whom the tongue of Thy power spoke "Were it not for Thee, I would not have created the celestial spheres" - and by His family and companions, to ordain for me that which shall profit me in this world and the next.

order.why: Consider wonder as an aspiration rather than simply a difficulty to escape.
shortened: O Ali, thou didst seek deliverance from the ocean of wonderment, yet this station was besought of God, glorified be His majesty, by the Seal of the Prophets in His words "Lord, increase my wonderment in Thee."

order.why: Close the linked readings with remembrance joined to action.
shortened: I beseech Thee, O Cleaver of the Dawn and Subduer of the Winds, by Thy Prophets and Thy Messengers and Thy chosen ones and Thy loved ones, whom Thou hast made the emblems of Thy guidance amidst Thy creation and the banners of Thy triumph throughout Thy lands, and by the light that shone forth from the horizon of Hijaz, and whose radiance illuminated both Yathrib and Batha, and all that dwell in the world of creation, to assist Thy servants to remember and praise Thee and to act according to what Thou hast revealed in Thy Book.

order.why: Read the supplied call for authoritative, unbiased, reverent study.
shortened: They must strive to obtain, from sources that are authoritative and unbiased, a sound knowledge of the history and tenets of Islam--the source and background of their Faith--and approach reverently and with a mind purged from preconceived ideas the study of the Qur'an which, apart from the sacred scriptures of the Babi and Baha'i Revelations, constitutes the only Book which can be regarded as an absolutely authenticated Repository of the Word of God.

order.why: Consider how learners can develop the capacity to guide others.
shortened: First is the importance of the study of Islam - which subject is still new to the majority of the believers, but whose importance for a proper and sound understanding of the Cause is absolutely indispensable. ...the Guardian would certainly advise, and even urge the friends to make a thorough study of the Qur'an as the knowledge of this Sacred Scripture is absolutely indispensable for every believer who wishes to adequately understand and intelligently read the Writings of Baha'u'llah.

order.why: End with room for serious study proportionate to interest and capacity.

questions: What might change when a religious tradition is approached through its own scripture and the conduct it seeks to cultivate?
How do these passages connect mercy, education, and the reconciliation of peoples?
How should historical generalizations and reported conversations be read alongside explicit affirmations of faith?
What questions does Qur’an 21:107 raise about the meaning and reach of a mission described through mercy?
How do the accounts of hardship, protection, and patience complicate a reading focused only on outward success?
What would an informed, reverent, and open-minded study of Islam involve for you?

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 21:107 · A mission described through mercy
references.note: The Quranic Arabic Corpus presents parallel translations, including Pickthall’s rendering of the mission as mercy for the peoples. Read the verse alongside the compilation’s prayers, its descriptions of education, and its calls to overcome inherited hostility. This comparison returns to an Islamic primary text rather than treating later descriptions of Islam as a substitute for its scripture.

subjects.displayTitle: All things involved in all things: living through relationship
subjects.introduction: No atom, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, can succeed without help; everything in this world depends on the assistance of others. The universe is a single body whose members sustain one another, a tree whose leaves and fruit flourish only through the whole, a chain in which no link can be loosened without disordering existence. Even the elements of a human body have journeyed through mineral, plant and animal before arriving, and will travel on, so that an old philosophers’ maxim holds: all things are involved in all things. Creatures feed on creatures, and plants breathe out what animals breathe in. Yet connection is real while the predictions of astrologers are not, and the chemistry of a century ago speaks in the vocabulary of its time. What the insight asks of a person is conduct: to see all humankind as leaves of one tree and to do, at every moment, some thoughtful kindness for one of them. Marcus Aurelius moves along a similar line, from a universe of connected things to membership in a common body that calls for beneficence [1]. From here the way leads into the necessary relationships that bind cause to effect, the need for cooperation, the person as a world in miniature, and the oneness of humanity.
subjects.arc: Begin with dependence and mutual care, explore change and connection, and return from the whole of existence to the life of one person.

order.why: Move from the world-tree to thoughtful help for another person.
shortened: Thus hath He likened this world of being to a single tree, and all its peoples to the leaves thereof, and the blossoms and fruits. It is needful for the bough to blossom, and leaf and fruit to flourish, and upon the interconnection of all parts of the world-tree, dependeth the flourishing of leaf and blossom, and the sweetness of the fruit.
Let them at all times concern themselves with doing a kindly thing for one of their fellows, offering to someone love, consideration, thoughtful help.

order.why: Open with the impossibility of succeeding without assistance.
Consider mutuality as a condition of life.
shortened: When we pounder deeply upon the connection and interdependence of beings, we clearly realize that the life of every being draws benefit and sustenance from all the other innumerable existences. This mutual helpfulness is realized either directly or through mediation, and if for the twinkling of an eye, this confirmation and assistance does not descend upon the living being, that one will become non-existent, for all the existing things are linked together and draw help from each other. Therefore, the greatest foundation of the world of existence is this co-operation and mutuality.

order.why: Explore cooperation across the levels of created existence.
shortened: In surveying the vast range of creation thou shalt perceive that the higher a kingdom of created things is on the arc of ascent, the more conspicuous are the signs and evidences of the truth that co-operation and reciprocity at the level of a higher order are greater than those that exist at the level of a lower order. For example, the evident signs of this fundamental reality are more discernible in the vegetable kingdom than in the mineral, and still more manifest in the animal world than in the vegetable.

order.why: Read bodily health as an image of collective assistance.
shortened: The world of existence is like the human form - all its members and parts, even to the finest and most delicate veins and nerves, must assist one another so that the collective body may attain health, well-being, comfort and life.

Observe how throughout all creation these divine connections, this universal order and divine law are in operation. Consider the plant, which releases an element that gives life to animals, while animals provide an element that causes the growth and development of plants. Thus, cooperation and mutual assistance are evident and manifest among all created things.

order.why: Consider how a single stone affects an entire building.
Trace both internal connections and dependence on outside influences.
shortened: It is obvious that all created things are connected one to another by a linkage complete and perfect, even, for example, as are the members of the human body. Note how all the members and component parts of the human body are connected one to another. In the same way, all the members of this endless universe are linked one to another.

Furthermore, although all created things grow and develop, yet are they subjected to influences from without. For instance, the sun giveth heat, the rain nourisheth, the wind bringeth life, so that man can develop and grow. Thus it is clear that the human body is under influences from the outside, and that without those influences man could not grow.

order.why: Examine the argument from composition and causal relationships.
shortened: For all beings are linked together like a chain; and mutual aid, assistance, and interaction are among their intrinsic properties and are the cause of their formation, development, and growth. It is established through numerous proofs and arguments that every single thing has an effect and influence upon every other, either independently or through a causal chain.

order.why: Read the whole universe through the image of a connected body.
shortened: My meaning, instead, is that this endless universe is like the human body and that all its parts are connected one with another and are linked together in the utmost perfection. That is, in the same way that the parts, members and organs of the human body are interconnected, and that they mutually assist, reinforce and influence each other, so too are the parts and members of this endless universe connected with, and spiritually and materially influenced by, one another.

order.why: Consider essential relationships as a trust.
Follow the inquiry from one influence to further causes.
shortened: In fine, that Universal Reality with all its qualities and attributes that we recount is holy and exalted above all minds and understandings. As we, however, reflect with broad minds upon this infinite universe, we observe that motion without a motive force, and an effect without a cause are both impossible; that every being hath come to exist under numerous influences and continually undergoeth reaction. These influences, too, are formed under the action of still other influences.

order.why: Distinguish relationships, their manifestation, and will.
Read the related account of every affair’s necessary relationships.
Consider the chain through the reported language of order and wisdom.
Compare connections within a person and within the universe.
shortened: We compare the body of the universe with the body of man. The members of the body of man are closely connected; so, also, are the parts of the great universe. The great events which happen are due to this connection. There is day, there is night; sometimes there are eclipses, etc.--all according to the requirements of this Divine system. All the created beings are connected with each other, and all occurrences and events are indicative of the requirements of this connection and interrelation.

order.why: Retain the reported account of small and great events.
shortened: Question: Are great calamities like this flood, the San Francisco earthquake, etc., caused by the wickedness of the people?

Answer: It belongs to the lesson of yesterday. Events like these happen because of the connection between the parts of the universe, for every small part has connection with every great part, and what affects one affects the other or all others.

order.why: Read the related statement of divine wisdom in occurrences.
Distinguish material reciprocity from spiritual influence attributed to stars.
shortened: O handmaid of God! The stars in the sky do not exert any spiritual influence on this world of dust; but all the members and parts of the universe are very strongly linked together in that limitless space, and this connection produceth a reciprocity of material effects.

order.why: Keep the caution about astrologers beside the affirmation of connection.
Read the historical astronomical vocabulary without treating it as a current scientific account.
Examine the analogy used in the answer about palmistry alongside the neighboring cautions about prediction.
shortened: Regarding palmistry: since all things, all beings that are members of this great body of the world of existence, are all interconnected - meaning each being is a member or part of that great body - therefore from any part, due to this connection, the realities of other parts can be discovered. Its analogy is the human body - imagine the world of possibility as a human body whose parts, members, elements and faculties are all interconnected with each other, having perfect connection.

order.why: Begin the sequence on matter’s movement with a flower’s changing elements.
Follow composition and dissolution through the argument for shared material existence.
shortened: Thus the existence and non-existence of created things consisteth of combination and dissolution. When the individual elements of a body are dissolved, each element combineth with other elements and another created thing cometh into being. Therefore every individual element progresseth through all ranks, and this is self-evident and sensible rather than a matter of belief. From this it is established that every individual element journeyeth through all created things.
Thus all created things exist in all created things. Consider what unity this is, that every particle of creation compriseth all creation.

order.why: Read the extended account of elements, forms, and their varied capacities.
shortened: Fundamentally all existing things pass through the same degrees and phases of development, and any given phenomenon embodies all others. An ancient statement of the Arabian philosophers declares that all things are involved in all things.

Whenever it appears in any distinct form or image, it has its opportunities, virtues and functions. As each component atom or element in the physical organisms of existence is subject to transference through endless forms and stages, possessing virtues peculiar to those forms and stations, it is evident that all phenomena of material being are fundamentally one.

order.why: Retain the concise statement of limitless transitions.
Read the reported philosophical maxim with its original physical terminology.
Return to the flower as a concrete example of changing forms.
Consider renewal as part of the order of nature.
Read gradual bodily decomposition within the passage’s account of material relationships.
shortened: And just as the composition, the formation, and growth and development of the physical body have come about by degrees, so too must its decomposition and dispersal be gradual. If the disintegration be rapid, this will cause an overleaping and a slackening in the chain of transferences, and this discontinuity will impair the universal relationships within the chain of created things.

order.why: Face the dependence of living creatures upon one another for nourishment.
shortened: For every part of the universe is connected with every other part by ties that are very powerful and admit of no imbalance, nor any slackening whatever.
For all creatures are eaters and eaten, and the very fabric of life is reared upon this fact. Were it not so, the ties that interlace all created things within the universe would be unravelled.

order.why: Consider the reported image of one form’s loss sustaining another.
Read reciprocal nourishment while retaining the source’s historical chemical vocabulary.
shortened: If for one instant this mutual helpfulness and co-operation were cut off from the sources and realities of things, all the existent beings and things would be thrown into confusion and chaos and be reduced to nothingness and annihilation. For instance, from the breath of the animals a watery element, called hydrogen, and carbon is exhaled and this is the life principle of the vegetable kingdom. From the vegetable kingdom and the trees, a fiery element, called oxygen, is emitted and this becomes the cause of the maintenance of the life of the animal kingdom. In such a manner, mutual helpfulness and co-operation is realized continually between all the existent beings.

order.why: Compare the related reported account of plants, animals, and a single body.
shortened: Answer: "All are connected by the bond of existence. What greater bond is there than this? Furthermore, none of these can continue to exist independently of the other; for interrelation and solidarity make their existence possible.

So are all the other beings (connected) making the world of existence as one person - a great person. Just as the members and parts of man co-operate and work together, likewise the parts and members of the world co-operate with each other and are interdependent.

order.why: Recognize shared feeling in the animal and human realms.
Consider the reported distinction between degrees of existence without confusing it with the transfer of matter.
Read the question of whether the chain ends with humanity.
Keep the reported explanation of transformation distinct from the divine Essence.
Consider an image of unity that retains individuality.
shortened: Taking the material ocean as an illustration, 'Abduil-Baha said, The atoms composing an ocean are, in appearance the ocean, but the identity of the atoms remains. So it is with our individuality in the ocean of life, it remains.

order.why: Hear the concise image of an invisible connection.
Read the factory analogy as an argument about an organizing power.
Compare the related analogy of soul, body, and machinery.
shortened: Likewise, observe factories and workshops, where all the machinery is connected to one another with interaction between them, yet connected to a general power which is the mover and axis of these interactions, namely steam power.

Thus it becomes clear that the interaction between created things, the cooperation and mutual assistance between elements, and the composition and analysis between beings are all connected to a moving power which is the axis and mover of creation.

order.why: Explore correspondence between spiritual and material realities.
Read the reported chain from outward appearance toward spiritual meaning.
Consider the reported connection between thought and outward form.
Attend to the experience of a landscape without turning it into literal speech.
Read communication through affection, light, rain, and growth.
Compare letters and a meaningful Word.
Consider participation in the whole through the particular.
Read the invitation to perceive signs inwardly and in every atom.
Retain the reported distinction between hidden reality and visible symbol.
Acknowledge degrees of unity that exceed description.
Pause with the concise affirmation of a world beheld in unity.
shortened: The world is the world of divine unity, and all are beheld on one plane.

order.why: Read common origin through tree, ocean, and existence.
Describes attraction and integration as conditions of life throughout existence.
Hear the shared gifts of sunlight and rain.
Consider every creature’s participation in a vast scene of life.
Bring the contemplation of all things back to the value of one soul.
shortened: And since in everything can be seen the attributes of all things, therefore upon a single one is conferred the decree of all. And this is the mystery of that which was formerly inspired in the Manifestation of My Self: "Whoso quickeneth a soul is as though he had quickened all mankind." For since all that is in the world existeth in a single soul, He therefore saith that if someone giveth life to a soul it is as though he had given life to all mankind, and if someone killeth a soul it is as though he had killed all the world.

order.why: Read the call to translate connection into fellowship and peace.
Close the linked readings with the reported hope that understanding oneness would end fighting.
shortened: What I discussed this morning was evident as the sun. That was the oneness of the existence of phenomena. But the first remarks were difficult of understanding, and most of the people did not understand what I was talking about, but some day I will make it clear to you. If the people should understand this aright, they would never war, they would never fight.

order.why: Retain the supplied fragment on created things as letters and words.
Keep the supplied pilgrim account of communication clearly attributed.
Read the supplied philosophical maxim in its original wording.
Consider the supplied account of necessary relationships without assigning blame for hardship.
End with the supplied Plotinian image of distinct parts in a common order.

questions: Which relationships sustain an ordinary day of your life while usually remaining unnoticed?
How do the body, tree, chain, and changing elements illuminate different kinds of connection?
How can the recognition of interdependence guide conduct without making every claim about hidden influence credible?
What changes when helping another is understood as participating in a common life?
How does Marcus Aurelius connect the order of the whole with cooperation, and where do the traditions’ accounts of divinity differ?
What might attention to one person’s welfare reveal about responsibility for humanity as a whole?

references.label: 1 · Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VII.9 and VII.13 · An ordered whole and mutual service
references.note: In George Long’s translation, VII.9 describes things as mutually connected within one ordered universe; VII.13 relates membership in a common body to cooperation and heartfelt beneficence. Compare this movement from cosmic connection to conduct with the compilation’s images of mutual aid. Marcus’s Stoic account of a divinity pervading the whole should remain distinct from Baha’i accounts of the divine Essence and creation.

subjects.displayTitle: Soul and body: a connection beyond containment
subjects.introduction: Someone says I went there, I decided this, and a second reality is speaking. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s teaching about that reality turns on a single distinction: the soul is connected with the body, not contained in it. The sun does not enter the mirror, yet the mirror is bright with it, and when the mirror breaks the sun is unharmed; the spirit sees by means of the eye and hears by means of the ear. Because the body is an instrument, no sword is blamed for a killing, and sin and kindness belong to the spirit. Because the connection is real, illness and age can veil the soul’s expression without diminishing it, and bodily care still matters. Second Corinthians, with its outward man perishing while the inward man is renewed day by day, offers a language of hope [1]. From here the inquiry opens toward the human soul as mirror, the mind as intermediary between soul and body, and the spirit after death, when individuality endures and the only question left is how far it has grown.
subjects.arc: Begin with identity and the mirror’s light, examine perception and bodily change, and consider enduring individuality and spiritual development.

order.why: Retain the concise account of an immaterial spirit connected to the body.
shortened: The spirit is absolutely placeless and immaterial, but it has a connection with the body, even as the sun has a connection with this mirror: The sun occupies no place within the mirror but it has a connection with it.

order.why: Open with the familiar experience of saying I and deliberating within oneself.
Introduce connection without physical entrance through the sun and mirror.
shortened: It has no need to enter or exit, ascend or descend, penetrate or commingle, for these are the properties of bodies, not of souls. Therefore, the soul of man does not enter into this corporeal frame, but rather it has a connection to it. Death consists of the severing of that connection. That connection resembles the relationship between a mirror and the sun. The sun does not enter into or depart from the mirror, and does not incarnate itself therein, but has a connection to the mirror and is reflected within it. When that connection becomes severed, the mirror is deprived of its brilliance, loveliness, and charm.

order.why: Clarify why language of entry and movement can be metaphorical.
Read the criticism of literal penetration in its source setting.
Consider the consequences for the image of transferring a soul between vessels.
shortened: They conceive of the body as a vessel and the spirit as its contents, like water and cup, with the water being emptied from one cup and poured into another.  This is indeed a childish notion:  They do not reflect deeply enough to realize that the spirit is an entirely incorporeal thing, that it does not enter or exit, and that at most it is connected with the body as the sun is with the mirror.

order.why: Distinguish bodily proximity from the conditions of spiritual manifestation.
Question spatial language applied to spiritual realities.
Read the related reported image of illumination without entrance.
shortened: The human spirit is not within the body; because it is exalted above all egress and ingress, above all circling and turning which only appertains to the essence (nature) of matter. The human spirit (or the soul) is a ray, a reflex out of God, and the relationship of the spirit and body is like that of the sun and the mirror. The spirit illumines the body.

order.why: Keep the brief question and answer on death as a severed connection.
Read the body’s deprivation when the relationship is severed.
Retain the reported version of the mirror analogy.
shortened: Spirit shines through the body as the sun is reflected in the mirror. The spirit is like the sun--it has a connection with the body like that of the sun to the mirror.
The mirror is lighted by the sun, and when the connection is broken the mirror becomes dark.

order.why: Consider why a broken mirror need not imply an extinguished sun.
shortened: The sun is reflected in the mirror; the mirror reflects the light and brilliancy of the sun, but the sun does not reside in the mirror. It does not enter nor come out of the mirror, nevertheless one sees it in the mirror, so the soul reflects itself in the body. If the mirror be broken the sun does not die. The body is the temporary mirror; the spiritual soul suffers no change, no more than the sun does remaining eternally in its own station.

order.why: Examine perception through bodily instruments.
shortened: Know that the influence and perception of the human spirit is of two kinds; that is, the human spirit has two modes of operation and understanding. One mode is through the mediation of bodily instruments and organs. Thus it sees with the eye, hears with the ear, speaks with the tongue. These are actions of the spirit and operations of the human reality, but they occur through the mediation of bodily instruments. Thus, it is the spirit that sees, but by means of the eye; it is the spirit that hears, but by means of the ear; it is the spirit that speaks, but by means of the tongue.

order.why: Compare the two modes of operation proposed in the account of waking and dreams.
shortened: The spirit has two modes of operation: one through instruments and means, that is, seeing through the eye, hearing through the ear, speaking through the tongue. Though these instruments are at work, it is the spirit that moves them. Though these powers appear through the body, they are through the power of the spirit. The other operation is without instruments, as in the world of dreams where one sees without eyes, hears without ears, speaks without tongue, and travels without moving the feet.

order.why: Read the related reported account of seeing and hearing during sleep.
Consider the argument from dreams with its original theological purpose.
Distinguish the outward senses, inward powers, and their mediation.
Read the extended distinction between changing mental expression and the soul.
shortened: Now concerning mental faculties, they are in truth of the inherent properties of the soul, even as the radiation of light is the essential property of the sun. The rays of the sun are renewed but the sun itself is ever the same and unchanged. Consider how the human intellect develops and weakens, and may at times come to naught, whereas the soul changeth not. For the mind to manifest itself, the human body must be whole; and a sound mind cannot be but in a sound body, whereas the soul dependeth not upon the body. It is through the power of the soul that the mind comprehendeth, imagineth and exerteth its influence, whilst the soul is a power that is free. The mind comprehendeth the abstract by the aid of the concrete, but the soul hath limitless manifestations of its own.

order.why: Consider coordination and the effects of interruption.
shortened: And each one of these members hath its own special function. The mind force -- whether we call it pre-existent or contingent -- doth direct and co-ordinate all the members of the human body, seeing to it that each part or member duly performeth its own special function. If, however, there be some interruption in the power of the mind, all the members will fail to carry out their essential functions, deficiencies will appear in the body and the functioning of its members, and the power will prove ineffective.

order.why: Read mutual assistance among bodily parts through the reported image of an organizing power.
Retain the concise statement of the spirit’s awareness of bodily sensations.
shortened: He both senses and comprehends it, for the spirit encompasses the body and is aware of its sensations and powers.

order.why: Read unseen agency through visible effects.
Consider the outward form as an expression of inward reality.
shortened: And yet, God be praised, despite their physical weaknesses, despite their feeble powers, these trials were steadfastly withstood, these tribulations overcome. Thus doth the body obey the spirit and the outer form reflect the inner reality.

order.why: Read the lamp as an instrument that needs illumination.
shortened: The body without spirit is not capable of real accomplishment. Although it may be in the utmost condition of beauty and excellence, it is, nevertheless, in need of the spirit. The chimney of the lamp, no matter how polished and perfect it be, is in need of the light. Without the light, the lamp or candle is not illuminating.

order.why: Keep the statement about causes dependent upon the rational soul.
Consider the body’s composition and animal life.
shortened: That is, the body of man, which is composed of the elements, is the most perfect form of composition and combination, the soundest arrangement, the noblest composition, and the most perfect of all existing things. It grows and develops through the animal spirit.

order.why: Retain the reported image of tension among the body’s component elements.
Read the argument from a repeated combination of elements within its philosophical setting.
shortened: As the completeness of man stems entirely from the component elements, their measure, their manner of combination, and the mutual action and interaction of other beings--and since man was produced ten or a hundred thousand years ago from the same earthly elements, with the same measures and quantities, the same manner of composition and combination, and the same interactions with other beings--it follows that man was exactly the same then as exists now. This is a self-evident truth and cannot be doubted. And if a thousand million years hence, the component elements of man are brought together, measured out in the same proportion, combined in the same manner, and subjected to the same interaction with other beings, exactly the same man will come into existence.

order.why: Explore why spiritual powers become manifest through a bodily composition.
shortened: Beyond this, the members, constituent parts and composition that are found within man attract and act as a magnet for the spirit: the spirit is bound to appear in it. Thus, when a mirror is polished, it is bound to attract the rays of the sun, to be illumined, and to reflect splendid images. That is, when these physical elements are gathered and combined together, according to the natural order and with the utmost perfection, they become a magnet for the spirit, and the spirit will manifest itself therein with all its perfections.

order.why: Read potentiality and individuality in the reported seed-and-tree analogy.
shortened: The existence of the tree within the seed is potential; but when the seed is sown and watered, the signs thereof, its roots and branches, and all of its different qualities, appear. Likewise the "rational soul" has a potential existence before its appearance in the human body, and through the mixture of elements and a wonderful combination, according to the natural order, law, conception and birth, it appears with its identity.

order.why: Keep the reported answer about prior existence distinct from an account of prior earthly personality.
Examine enduring individuality and the body’s dependence upon the soul.
shortened: The rational soul---the human spirit---did not descend into this body or subsist through it to begin with, that it should require some substance to depend upon after the constituent parts of the body have decomposed. On the contrary, the rational soul is the substance upon which the body depends. The rational soul is endowed from the beginning with individuality; it does not acquire it through the intermediary of the body. At most, what can be said is that the individuality and identity of the rational soul may be strengthened in this world, and that it may either progress and attain to the degrees of perfection or remain in the lowest abyss of ignorance and be veiled from and deprived of beholding the signs of God.

order.why: Consider the reported refusal to dissolve individuality into an undifferentiated whole.
Distinguish physical perception from the spiritual capacities asserted in the passage.
Read discovery as an illustration of powers extending beyond immediate sense perception.
Keep the reported humor about a salad beside the account of intellectual and spiritual discovery.
Acknowledge the body’s contribution to the expression of mental powers.
Consider the reported reciprocity of bodily and inward joy.
Hear encouragement offered to someone with physical weakness.
Read spiritual fortitude as assistance amid hardship.
Consider the reported connection between inward harmony and action.
shortened: But if there is a harmony in man, a quiet concord, in brief, a unity between voluntary and involuntary processes, between conscious and unconscious will, then there will result an agreement of human and divine will, or better: a unification of the human will-to-action with the eternal will of God, which results in the tranquillity of the conscience of man, his highest earthly good.

order.why: Keep the reported correction of an ascetic interpretation in its conversational setting.
Distinguish a temporary reduction in passion through deprivation from a lasting change of character.
Locate moral agency and responsibility beyond the bodily instrument.
shortened: As to the body, it is but an instrument for the spirit, for it is the spirit that moveth, acteth, acquireth, committeth both good and evil. Sin and righteousness, cruelty and kindliness spring from the soul and spirit, not from the helpless body.

No sword is called to account for slaying the innocent, and no arrow is reproached for wounding the helpless, for these are but instruments, not agents; they are governed, not governors; they are subdued, not subduing.

order.why: Read the reported concern about identification with material impulses.
shortened: When we speak of the soul we mean the motive power of this physical body which lives under its entire control in accordance with its dictates. If the soul identifies itself with the material world it remains dark, for in the natural world there is corruption, aggression, struggles for existence, greed, darkness, transgression and vice.

order.why: Consider the soul’s fruitfulness through its relation to spirit.
Compare the reported account of the soul as an intermediary.
Retain the source’s distinct terminology for soul, spirit, mind, and body.
Distinguishes the spirit’s continuity from changes and injury to the body.
Read the reported account of an ethereal body without forcing it into the vocabulary of other passages.
Acknowledge the reported distinction between a bodily injury and the experience of pain.
Read spiritual strength amid bodily difficulty without denying suffering or care.
shortened: We see that cold, heat, suffering, etc, only concern the body, they do not touch the spirit.

How often do we see a man, poor, sick, miserably clad, and with no means of support, yet spiritually strong. Whatever his body has to suffer, his spirit is free and well! Again, how often do we see a rich man, physically strong and healthy, but with a soul sick unto death.

order.why: Consider how illness can veil expression without extinguishing spiritual reality.
shortened: Likewise, in illness the manifestation of the spirit's power and might is prevented and veiled due to intervening causes, but after its release from the body it appears with such power, might and ascendancy as cannot be imagined. The pure, holy and sanctified spirits have ever possessed and shall continue to possess all power and complete freedom.

order.why: Read bodily loss alongside the affirmation of an undiminished soul.
shortened: The body weakens, but the soul is not affected. The body becomes incapacitated or paralyzed, but the soul suffers no change. No matter how many of man s limbs become amputated, the condition of the soul is unvarying and undergoes no change whatsoever.

order.why: Keep the stated distinction between bodily condition and the soul’s state.
Compare rider and lantern images in the account of bodily change.
Read the related argument concerning physical impairments.
Attend to the reported words addressed to a person who had lost both legs.
Follow the argument from particular bodily changes to bodily dissolution.
Keep the reported discussion of aging focused on functional organs rather than essential worth.
Read the reported emphasis on enduring spirit in a reflection on Christ’s suffering.
shortened: Bodily matters are not important. The physical suffering of Christ passed away, but his spirit was everlasting. These bodily sufferings come and pass away, but the spirit is eternal. The body is not important. The spirit is important.

order.why: Understand the brief contrast of importance within its spiritual argument.
shortened: For the body of man is accidental; it is of no importance. The time of its disintegration will inevitably come. But the spirit of man is essential and, therefore, eternal.

order.why: Retain the reported claim about consciousness after death as attributed.
shortened: The physical body of man is like that of the animal, the only difference being on the level of consciousness. It follows therefore that only consciousness or mind is left after death.

order.why: Read the reported expectation of life freed from present material conditions.
shortened: Here we are subject to the conditions of matter; after this will succeed life on the mental plane, a life freed from this material body.

order.why: Distinguish passing physical features from enduring divine qualities.
Consider love as a fire that bodily dissolution cannot quench.
shortened: As to the soul which is intended, in truth it hath been called forth by the Word of God and is such that, if it be kindled with the fire of the love of its Lord, neither the waters of opposition nor the oceans of the world can quench its flame. That soul is indeed a fire ablaze in the tree of man which proclaimeth: "No God is there but Him!"
And when it casteth off its earthly frame, God shall raise it up again in the most excellent of forms and cause it to enter a sublime paradise.

order.why: Read the bird-and-cage argument from sleep toward continued existence.
shortened: Our body is like the cage, and the spirit is like the bird. We see that without the cage this bird flies in the world of sleep; therefore, if the cage becomes broken, the bird will continue to exist; its feelings will be even more powerful, its perceptions greater and its happiness increased.

order.why: Hear consolation through the image of a freed bird.
shortened: Like a bird in the cage of this body he was captive and confined. This cage was broken and that bird took flight, becoming intimate and harmonious with the divine birds in the celestial garden.

order.why: Keep the related reported words of consolation in their setting.
shortened: The very utmost is this, he was imprisoned in this material cage, he was like unto a bird, he was in the troubles of this life enduring its vicissitudes. He broke this cage and flew away. From this terrestrial [plane] he ascended to the heavenly rose-garden. From this darkened world he ascended to the world of illumination.

order.why: Read freedom and peace through the nightingale’s song.
Close the linked readings with the image of word and meaning.
Retain the supplied reminder that bodily soundness can support expression.
Read the supplied scholarly account of outward and inward powers as commentary.
Compare the supplied Plotinian account of soul and embodiment.
Consider the net and sea as another account of presence beyond size.
End with the supplied philosophical definition and its acknowledged limits.
shortened: The best, most perfect, and clearest of these is that spirit is an abstract substance separate from matter in essence but not in act.

Spirit cannot be described by such attributes as ingress and egress, independence and inherence, advance and retreat, movement and stillness. Eyes cannot perceive it, nor can the other senses. Yet it remains in need of matter in all acts, and inseparable from it in all conditions, for it is unimaginable that matter be stripped from it. No act can issue from spirit except through matter, and it is inconceivable that an effect could be produced by spirit save through the instrumentality of matter.

questions: What do the different images of soul and body reveal, and what might each image leave unexplained?
How does connection differ from containment in these passages?
How can enduring spiritual worth be affirmed while taking bodily suffering, disability, and care seriously?
What distinctions emerge between the soul, its expression through mental powers, and the instruments of perception?
How does Second Corinthians 4:16–18 illuminate inward renewal amid outward change without settling every philosophical question here?
What might the possibility of continuing individuality imply for how identity and character are developed now?

references.label: 1 · 2 Corinthians 4:16–18 · Inward renewal and outward change
references.note: The King James Version contrasts outward decline with daily inward renewal and directs attention toward what endures beyond the visible. Compare that movement with the compilation’s distinction between spiritual reality and its bodily expression. The Christian passage offers a language of hope amid suffering; it should not be treated as a complete account of the Baha’i understanding of soul, mind, and body.

subjects.displayTitle: Pilgrimage: the journey and its inward fruits
subjects.introduction: Two kinds of traveller reach the Holy Land, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá once said: pilgrims and tourists, and only the first go home with hearts that have become caskets for the jewels of God. Pilgrimage is a law of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas, ordained for those who are able, and the counsel surrounding it is strikingly practical: one must have the means, must not leave a family in need, must wait for permission and for a year when the land is at peace, and whoever cannot come is told that service night and day is the same as visiting the holy places. Within those limits runs a longing almost unbearable: Bahá’u’lláh’s wish for a single handful of dust from the City He could not reach. The Qur’án joins pilgrimage to remembrance, benefit and feeding the needy [1], and the same generosity appears here in prayers offered at the Threshold for relatives who stayed behind. The question that remains is what returns home with the traveller. The path leads onward into the Shrines and holy places, the meaning of permission to visit, the prayers said for pilgrims, and the Hajj of Islam.
subjects.arc: Begin with inward purpose, read law alongside capacity and circumstance, and follow the traveler from preparation to gratitude and service.

order.why: Open with the reported distinction between an inward pilgrimage and a visit to places.
shortened: In this Cause there are two kinds of travelers - pilgrims and tourists. The pilgrims are those who after the visit to the Holy Tomb are surrounded with the Glances of the Mercy of the Almighty, their hearts become the caskets for the Jewels of the Treasury of God, and their spirits stirred by the Breaths of the Holy Spirit; but the tourists are those who just come to see the places, showing in all things a historic interest and probably after their departure they will write a booklet.

order.why: Place the law and its stated qualification at the center of the practical readings.
Consider pilgrimage engaging inward and outward life together.
Ask what gifts the traveler may bring home to others.
shortened: O handmaiden of God! The Divine Physician of hearts and the Healer of bodies and souls arrived at the Luminous Threshold with perfect eagerness and joy, and his arrival became the cause of delight to the essences of being.

The influence of this pilgrimage will become evident and manifest in the future, for when he returns from this rose garden, he will, God willing, take with him the holy fragrances and the sweet scents of intimacy as a gift.

order.why: Read service as a form of nearness when travel must wait.
Consider the need for means and the consequences of avoidable hardship.
Read preparedness through the hope of traveling with tranquility.
Keep a postponement within its particular circumstances.
Attend to family needs and illness in the decision to return.
shortened: The honored Afnans of the Sacred Tree were with us for some time and were blessed to visit the Pure Shrine. The intention was that they would be blessed with the great bounty of circumambulation here longer, but due to your being alone, and especially since Mirza Badi' mentioned some slight illness, therefore the honored ones requested to return.

order.why: Distinguish visiting the Shrines from the presence of Abdu’l-Baha.
Read distinctions among places and obligations in the source’s historical setting.
Keep the instruction addressed to residents of Shiraz within its specific context.
Consider the alternative use of resources otherwise spent on special journeys to graves.
Read the earlier statement that the ordinance remained concealed.
Keep the reported explanation of Babi and Baha’i provisions in its historical setting.
Read the Bab’s ordinance with its own terminology and promises.
Consider the House of Him Whom God shall make manifest within the Arabic Bayan.
Retain the Bab’s language of visitation and reward with the supplied omission visible.
Hear longing for a sanctuary when access has been prevented.
shortened: To thee do I voice My plaint regarding those who prevented me from visiting thee and arriving at the carpet of thy glory. For by Him in Whose hand is my soul, if God were to give me all that is on earth, I would give it to enter your sanctuary, for it is a piece of the gardens of Paradise and its ruling flows according to the ruling of the Holy One in the blessed spot for those who behold with their own eyes the ruling of the Bayan.

order.why: Read the reported announcement of the Bab’s journey to Hijaz.
shortened: As to Myself, I shall, accompanied by Quddus and My Ethiopian servant, proceed on My pilgrimage to Hijaz. I shall join the company of the pilgrims of Fars, who will shortly be sailing for that land. I shall visit Mecca and Medina, and there fulfil the mission with which God has entrusted Me.

order.why: Consider the Bab’s letter describing arrival and circumambulation.
shortened: On the first day of Dhi'l-Hijjih I was honored to reach the House of God. I stayed twenty-seven days in that sacred land and performed the circumambulation of the House on behalf of the owners. May God in His grace and mercy accept it.

order.why: Keep the Medina letter’s testimony and warning within its address.
Read the request concerning a House and the verses recited upon return.
shortened: Therefore, O thou present one in the city, ask my mother -- if she be content -- then appoint someone to restore the exterior of the House with stones of righteousness, for it is indeed an ancient House. Then charge one skilled in the naskh hand to inscribe with gold the Surah of Ria¸van upon twelve gilded leaves; for I desire that what is commonly recited at the pilgrims' return be replaced with the verses of truth.

order.why: Hear the reported appreciation of pilgrims traveling on foot.
shortened: He praised the manner and the devotion of the old Pilgrims with distaff in hand, making the journey to the holy Shrines on foot. He delivered himself of the opinion that throughout all his life he has been longing to visit Mecca.

order.why: Consider the blessed places of Yathrib and Batha.
shortened: Blessed is the soul that hath turned for the sake of God and attained the fragrance of Yathrib and Batha. The divine fragrances waft from those lands and the light of His Cause shineth forth from its horizon.

order.why: Read the Qur’anic duty through its stated condition of ability.
Follow the movement from hearing a command to undertaking a journey.
shortened: After hearkening to the blessed word "Pilgrimage to the House is a duty unto God for mankind," he turned toward the divine command until he attained the privilege of visiting the Most Great House of God.

order.why: Consider the attraction of the command amid hardship.
Read the longer praise of the word that draws people across great distances.
shortened: Praise be sanctified above the ways of the peoples of the world and the intimations of all who dwell within the realm of possibility, befitting that omnipotent Sovereign Who, through the blessed Word "Pilgrimage to the House is incumbent upon men for the sake of God," hath in every year so attracted and drawn vast multitudes that they forsake their children, their offspring, their wealth and all they possess, and with a hundred thousand longings and yearnings endure the hardships and calamities of land and sea, of desert and mountain, that they might attain to that Spot which is the object of that blessed Word.

order.why: Keep desire, permission, and prayer together.
Consider pilgrimage as an act undertaken for the sake of obedience.
Read the Most Great Pilgrimage through its focus on the divine Manifestation.
Clarifies that pilgrimage to either of the two designated Houses suffices.

sourceQuestion.text: 29. QUESTION:  Again inquiry hath been made about the pilgrimage.

order.why: Consider outward washing joined to an inward petition for purity.
Read preparation and praise as part of the approach.
Enter the earlier visitation text through remembrance and intention.
shortened: When thou arrivest at the gate of the first sanctuary, pause and magnify thy Lord God as thou turnest thy face toward His face, and say: "O my God! I have sought Thee through Thyself and desired Thy proof through that wherewith Thou hast called me by Thy mercy.
Then enter with effaced verses and manifest signs, for if in that station thou callest to mind any remembrance save the remembrance of thy Lord, the angel will cry out "Return!

order.why: Keep the reported restriction on prostration attached to its source and setting.
Hear the joy conveyed by permission to visit.
shortened: O thou who art yearning for the pathway of the Friend! Glad tidings upon glad tidings that thou art permitted to visit the Court of Divine Oneness, and a thousand joyous tidings that thou mayest don the pilgrim's garb to circumambulate the holy and purified Sanctuary.

order.why: Retain the request for permission on another’s behalf.
shortened: He seeks permission for thy presence in the blessed white spot and thy honor in pressing thy face upon the dust of the Most Exalted Threshold and covering thy brow with the luminous earth.

order.why: Consider the proposed shared journey and further visit to Persia.
Read hospitality as a material support for spiritual travel.
Follow the seeker across land and sea toward the desired presence.
Consider the longing that moves someone to leave home.
shortened: Blessed art thou for having forsaken thy home out of longing for the precincts of God, and for having turned toward that place wherefrom was raised the call in remembrance of thy Lord, the Mighty, the Loving. Thou didst hasten unto the Beloved until thou didst enter the sacred court and circumambulate the House.

order.why: Retain the concise account of arrival.
shortened: Thou didst depart and traverse the path until thou didst arrive at this Spot which God hath made the object of circumambulation for the Concourse on High and the angels brought nigh.

order.why: Read the journey to the Most Great Prison through its devotional purpose.
Hear thanksgiving for help throughout the journey.
shortened: O thou who art a pilgrim to the Holy Sepulcher, praised be God who hath aided, sustained and confirmed thee and bestowed upon thee His favors, fulfilled His mercy and removed thy sorrows. He hath guided thee throughout both land and sea, walked thee through vast ravines, deserts and valleys, enabled thee to enter the fragrant Holy Spot, and to circumambulate that Spot around which the Concourse on High have circled.

order.why: Consider effort and the reaching of a cherished goal.
shortened: O thou who hast visited the Most Exalted Shrine and circled round the Supreme Horizon! Praise be to God that thou hast made a worthy effort, traversed wilderness and desert, and reached thy goal. Thou hast laid thy brow at the Luminous Threshold and perfumed thy face and hair with the sacred dust of that Holy Court.

order.why: Keep the particular account of travel despite weakness alongside the earlier counsel about means.
shortened: O servant of God! His honor Shaykh Rahmani, despite extreme weakness, traversed great distances and endured the hardships and difficulties of travel until he arrived at the shore of the Holy Land and perfumed his nostrils with the dust of the threshold of the Holy Shrine.

order.why: Read the journey’s hardships and the imagery of an illumined heart.
shortened: O friend! His honor Haji endured the hardship of sea voyage and traversing the desert, ascending and descending mountains, and hastened forward eagerly toward the Blessed Spot until he pressed his forehead to the Luminous Threshold and his eyes were illumined by witnessing the Greater Signs, and his heart, like a rose garden and meadow, received great bounty from the favors of the Most Glorious.

order.why: Consider arrival through the image of a center of circles.
shortened: You traversed plain and desert, mountain and sea, and arrived at the true Ka'bah, the destination of the Beloved. You circumambulated around the center of infinite circles and perfumed your nostrils with the holy fragrances of the sacred dust.

order.why: Connect the outward journey with detachment and spiritual understanding.
Read renewed life as a fruit of arrival.
Hear gratitude voiced to a parent concerning a son’s pilgrimage.
Read the account of a husband’s journey as news shared with his wife.
Consider safety and shelter in a report sent home.
Hear a child addressed through the blessing associated with the parents’ journey.
Read the safe arrival of relatives through sacred-place imagery.
Consider prayer offered for a parent at the Threshold.
Read remembrance on behalf of someone absent.
Follow the widening circle of prayer to relatives and connections.
Consider flowers, humility, and visitation on others’ behalf.
Retain the particular report of representative visitation.
Read a request for prayers on Abdu’l-Baha’s behalf.
Hear the journey recounted in prayer.
Read approach to the Threshold as the opening of a personal petition.
shortened: O Lord! He has hastened to Your sacred precincts and arrived at the wellsprings of Your favors and been honored at the circumambulation point of the Supreme Concourse and visited the Most Holy and Exalted Spot and rubbed his forehead in the dust of Your pure Threshold and communed with You with his heart and spirit and being, saying: "Lord!

order.why: Consider reassurance that a journey and turning have been accepted.
shortened: The oceans of divine affection that surge within the hearts of spiritual souls are but a drop created, by His will, from the sea of His mercy. Be not thou sorrowful. Thy journey hath been accepted, thy turning approved, and the Tongue of God beareth witness that thy visitation at the Most Holy Court is adorned with the fairest of ornaments.

order.why: Hear the joy of arrival and spiritual aspiration.
shortened: O thou who art intoxicated with the wine of the Covenant! With the utmost joy and fragrance didst thou arrive at the blessed, luminous Shrine, where thou didst inhale the sweet fragrances from the rose-garden of the All-Merciful and attain to the ultimate hopes and spiritual desires.

order.why: Retain the personal account of hastening to the Threshold.
shortened: Therefore in these days he hastened from there to visit the Holy Threshold at this circumambulation point of the Supreme Concourse, and brightened his eyes and perfumed his nostrils from the dust of the pure threshold.

order.why: Read news of a pilgrim shared with a community.
Consider pilgrimage followed by another encounter in Egypt.
shortened: O divine friends! Jinab-i-Aqa Musa and Aqa Qanbar-'Ali traversed long distances, mountains, deserts and seas to reach the blessed and luminous Shrine. After attaining the presence at the Sacred Threshold, they hastened to the realm of Egypt and met with this center of poverty and nothingness.

order.why: Hear the account of Varqa’s time near the Shrine.
shortened: O you who gaze upon the Most Glorious Kingdom! His honor Mirza Varqa, upon him be the Glory of God the Most Glorious, has for some time been blessed with pilgrimage to the Holy Shrine and has been intimate with the holy fragrances.

order.why: Read visitation and companionship together.
shortened: You attained the presence of the Luminary of the horizons, circumambulated the gathering place of the Supreme Concourse, were blessed to visit the sacred and blessed Threshold of the Exalted One (may my spirit be sacrificed for Him), and associated with 'Abdu'l-Baha.

order.why: Consider repeated visits within a period of companionship.
shortened: Thou hast, for some time, been a companion of these enraptured souls and hast associated with these yearning ones in this Most Great Prison. Praise be to God, for thy brow hath been illumined and thy sight brightened by the dust of the sacred Shrine. Time and again, thou hast attained the honour of visiting the Exalted Threshold---that Spot round which circle the celestial Concourse, that Sanctuary of the denizens of the Abha Kingdom---and hast detected the sweet scents of holiness.

order.why: Follow the daily rhythm of gathering, remembrance, and visitation.
Retain the brief account of meeting friends and remaining in the Prison.
