shortened: O servant of God! For some time now you have been here and attained the blessing of visiting the Threshold that is the point of circumambulation of the Concourse on High, and met with the friends, and tarried in this Most Great Prison.

order.why: Read the gathering of travelers from different regions in its historical setting.
shortened: Now to the Holy Shrine, from every direction - from Iran, Turkistan, East and West, Europe and America - the friends are continuously arriving without any obstacle or hindrance. All are prostrate before `Abdu'l-Baha at the Holy Threshold in utmost supplication and entreaty, receiving infinite bounties.

order.why: Hear the reported welcome after a long journey.
Consider the reported importance of a welcome at the Threshold.
shortened: The Bahai friends traverse long distances in order to visit the Holy Tomb and to sense the fragrances of holiness. If they should arrive at the threshold and find the guardian away they would become sad and disheartened.

order.why: Read refuge and shelter as part of pilgrimage.
shortened: O Persian handmaiden of the Lord God! For some time you have been blessed to visit the holy dust of the Wronged One of the horizons, and you have rubbed your face and hair at the threshold of the court of the All-Knowing Lord and performed pilgrimage, finding shelter and refuge in the sacred precinct.

order.why: Consider remembrance at the Shrine as a source of joy amid sorrow.
Make practical service to pilgrims part of the journey’s meaning.
shortened: O distracted one! That radiant countenance - offer a hundred thousand thanks in every breath that you have become the companion of the lovers of the Beloved's face, and have traversed towns and wilderness and sea until you reached the blessed luminous spot, and circumambulated around the Most Great Sanctuary, and were blessed with the bounty of providing water for the pilgrims and [serving] the Sacred Mosque.

order.why: Hear thanksgiving for a particular group’s blessed journey.
Read the visit of Afnan through its language of divine bounty.
Retain the concise invitation to gratitude.
shortened: Give thanks unto God for having enabled thee to circumambulate the Most Great House and to attain unto the Most Great Pilgrimage.

order.why: Consider the devotional image of sacred places themselves longing for the pilgrim.
Read spiritual pilgrimage through imagery beyond ordinary place.
shortened: I bear witness that thou hast visited the Sanctuary of God and circumambulated the Holy Kaaba in the ascension of eternity above the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, nigh unto the Most Glorious and Most Luminous Pavilion - that Station beyond which all names and attributes are cut off.

order.why: Consider the inward state associated with nearness.
shortened: Therefore this condition in itself is the ultimate desire of lovers, and when the heat of this state surges in hearts, it merits the honor of circumambulating the Sacred Threshold.

order.why: Keep the reported suggestion that the full gift exceeds present understanding.
shortened: For example, one of the gifts of God is to be able to pay a visit to the Holy Tomb, but man cannot fully realize it while in this world. But when he enters the World of the Kingdom, there the blessings and gifts will become evident and clear.

order.why: Retain the response to disparagement of pilgrims in its polemical setting.
End with longing for the City and the pain of being prevented from returning.

questions: What distinguishes reaching a place from receiving the inward fruits of a journey?
How do means, safety, permission, and care for family enter the practice of devotion?
What can prayer on behalf of absent people reveal about the communal dimensions of pilgrimage?
How does Qur’an 22:28 connect sacred observance with benefit and care for people in need?
What kinds of service might express a desire for nearness when travel is impossible or postponed?
What changes in everyday life could carry the gifts of a pilgrimage home?

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 22:28 · Remembrance, benefit, and provision during pilgrimage
references.note: In Pickthall’s rendering, pilgrims witness benefit, remember God on appointed days over the cattle provided to them, and feed people in need. Compare the relationship of observance and shared benefit with these accounts of remembrance, hospitality, and service. The particular rites of Islamic Hajj remain distinct from the pilgrimage practices and historical instructions collected here.

subjects.displayTitle: Outward and inward meanings: reading with depth and fidelity
subjects.introduction: Whoever takes the outward meaning and abandons the inner is ignorant, Bahá’u’lláh teaches, and whoever takes the inner and abandons the outward is heedless; the sage holds both. The test He gives is almost comic in its plainness. If the Will of God says wash your faces, the face is to be washed with water, and whoever spiritualises it away may walk about with a dirty face while imagining himself devout. Yet the same Writings insist that bread, wine, heaven, the falling stars and the throne of David open into meanings no physical form can contain, and that the Jews of Jesus’ day knew the letter by heart while missing its life-giving spirit. Depth is real, and so is the temptation to use depth as an escape from what a text plainly asks. Jesus’ own explanation of the sower, in Mark 4:13–20, shows interpretation serving hearing and fruitfulness [1]. The path leads on into symbolism and literal interpretation, into the meanings of letters and numbers, and into the first and the last, the seen and the hidden, where outward life and inward purpose are asked to agree.
subjects.arc: Begin with the tension between depth and plain instruction, read examples of spiritual interpretation, and seek agreement between outward life and inward purpose.

order.why: Open with the need to hold outward and inward meanings together.
Test interpretation against the ordinary instruction to wash one’s face.
Explore the distinction between unveiled guidance and concealed language.
shortened: It is evident unto thee that the Birds of Heaven and Doves of Eternity speak a twofold language. One language, the outward language, is devoid of allusions, is unconcealed and unveiled; that it may be a guiding lamp and a beaconing light whereby wayfarers may attain the heights of holiness, and seekers may advance into the realm of eternal reunion.
The other language is veiled and concealed, so that whatever lieth hidden in the heart of the malevolent may be made manifest and their innermost being be disclosed.
In such utterances, the literal meaning, as generally understood by the people, is not what hath been intended.

order.why: Read the assertion that neither aspect need prevent the other.
Keep the warning against unsupported inward claims beside hope for inner meaning.
shortened: Interpret not the divine Word, and remain not veiled from its outer meaning, for none knoweth its interpretation save God and those who are heedless of the outer meaning of the words and claim to understand their inner meanings - I swear by the Most Great Name that such souls have been and shall ever be liars. Blessed are they who act upon the outer meaning and hope for the inner meaning.

order.why: Read the counsel to cleave to clear meaning in its source setting.
Consider how a literal interpretation may be affirmed while further meanings are explored.
Read the particular purpose assigned to outwardly expressed encouragement.
Read the two aspects of sacred words and the need for receptivity.
shortened: Know thou furthermore that each letter of these sacred words hath two aspects - one turning toward the inner meaning and one toward the outer. Would that we could find attentive ears and receptive hearts that could bear to hear the realities of meaning contained within God's Book and become illumined by the lights of the suns dawning from the horizons of God's words!

order.why: Consider inwardness and outwardness within a single command.
Keep the distinction between an apparent meaning and one that exceeds it.
Retain the Bab’s statement on revelation and interpretation in its own setting.
Read verses as a source of illumination.
Consider the differing voices of lawgiver, seeker, and mystic within one purpose.
shortened: So long, however, as the thick clouds of oppression, which obscure the daystar of justice, remain undispelled, it would  be difficult for the glory of this station to be unveiled to men's eyes. These thick clouds are the exponents of idle fancies and vain imaginings, who are none other but the divines of Persia. At one time We spoke in the language of the lawgiver; at another in that of the truth-seeker and the mystic, and yet Our supreme purpose and highest wish hath always been to disclose the glory and sublimity of this station.

order.why: Connect the purpose of revelation with perfections appearing in human life.
shortened: This Revelation hath not come to enforce earthly commandments, as were recorded in the Bayan by the Pen of the Merciful, but rather to manifest the evidences of perfection in human souls -- that their spirits may be lifted up to eternal stations and that which their minds can scarcely believe may brilliantly appear -- till all may ultimately tread above the kingdoms of earth and heaven.

order.why: Read the stated custom of mystics speaking outwardly while intending inward meanings.
Consider why allusion may sometimes speak more eloquently than an explicit statement.
Place humility and acknowledged limits beside the search for understanding.
Read the reported capacity to discover meanings beyond immediate visibility.
Consider the effort involved in penetrating inner significance.
shortened: To penetrate the inner significances a mighty effort is needed."
When one in reading substitutes the symbolic or spiritual title of the great ones, the human temple fades and only reality remains.

order.why: Begin the examples with bread as an image of heavenly bounty.
shortened: Everything that the Prophets foretold came to pass, but they were all allegories. Literal meanings were not intended, inasmuch as the Words of God are symbolic; they are mysteries. They are a treasure; treasures are hidden. They are a mine of gems; mines are always hidden. For example, Christ says, "I am the bread of heaven." It is obvious that Christ was not bread, and that to outward seeming He did not come from heaven; rather, He issued from the womb of Mary. By this "bread," however, is meant the bread of heavenly bounty---the celestial perfections.

order.why: Read the interpretation of Eucharistic language as the source’s account.
Compare the related explanation of the Supper and spiritual nourishment.
Consider birth and heaven as two perspectives upon the coming of Christ.
shortened: Now, just as He came the first time in appearance from the womb but in reality from heaven, so will He come the second time in appearance from the womb but in reality from heaven. The conditions that have been recorded in the Gospel for the second coming of Christ are indeed the same as had been specified for His first coming, as was explained before.

order.why: Read the relation of spiritual reality to Gospel descriptions.
Examine the stated spiritual interpretation of resurrection.
Retain the reported interpretation of fish, honeycomb, and resurrection.
Keep the concise reported claim about miracles in its attribution.
Compare the interpretation of raising the dead with the Exodus imagery.
Read the related reported account of the Red Sea as a spiritual journey.
shortened: The crossing of the Red Sea has a spiritual meaning. It was a spiritual journey, through, and above the sea of corruption and iniquity of Pharaoh and his people, or army. By the help of God, through Moses, the Israelites were able to cross this sea safely and reach the Promised Land (spiritual state), while Pharaoh and his people were drowned in their own corruption.

order.why: Distinguish allegorical verses from decisive ones in the treatment of Adam.
shortened: Therefore, we say that these verses indicating the disobedience of Adam, peace be upon him, or the error of certain Prophets, are allegorical verses, not decisive ones, and they have an interpretation in inspired hearts and hidden meanings with tranquil souls.

order.why: Consider the reported argument against a physical reading of falling stars.
shortened: Concerning the falling of the stars: Many of the stars are larger than the sun. The sun is a million times larger than the earth, and many of the Stars are larger than the sun. How then can they fall upon the earth? It is as if a hundred thousand mountains should be placed upon a grain of mustard. These are symbols only.

order.why: Explore more than one sense of heaven within the same commentary.
Retain the direction to read the Johannine chapter through inner meaning.
Read heavenly Jerusalem alongside the source’s affirmation of an outward gathering.
shortened: For this divine Jerusalem, at whose center lies the Holy of Holies, is the heavenly city and celestial metropolis. East and West lie in but one of its corners.
Nevertheless, in the outward sense too, Israel shall gather in the Holy Land, and this is a promise that shall not prove false.

order.why: Consider bride and bridegroom as scriptural symbols.
Hear the reported counsel to receive words in spirit.
Read the reported explanation of symbols in Baha’u’llah’s writings.
Consider how changing terminology can affect later understanding.
Keep the reported account of familiar stories and their use in its source setting.
Explore the different meanings assigned to choice wine.
shortened: By choice wine is meant at times the divine verses themselves, and at times His love - whoso drinketh thereof shall never thirst. This choice wine bestoweth life and conferreth eternal existence. In another sense, what is meant by it are the hidden pearls within the utterance of the Goal of all worlds, and its chalices are the writings revealed by the Supreme Pen.

order.why: Distinguish the value of meaning from the refinement of its vessel.
Read fresh and withered as terms interpreted through nearness and distance.
shortened: The primary meaning of "fresh" refers to utterances that draw man closer to the Truth, that is, bring him nearer to God, while "withered" is that which removes him from His straight path - namely the divines and theologians of the earth whom you see today lying prostrate as if they were hollow palm-trunks.

order.why: Retain the symbolic tree and its branches within the source’s address.
Distinguish spiritual sovereignty from earthly dominion.
Read the reported reign of Christ through its influence upon hearts.
Consider the throne of David as a reported image of heavenly authority.
shortened: Third: That he should sit on the throne of David. It is clear that he did not have a throne: he did not have even a mat to sit on. The throne of His Holiness is a heavenly throne, not a throne which is built of gold and silver.

order.why: Read the reported outward sacrifice as a sign of inward sacrifice.
Consider body and spirit through the image of word and meaning.
Read the lamp as an outward expression of inward light.
shortened: There is a Persian proverb: "The outer is the expression of the inner". For instance, this lamp is the outer, the light which it contains is the inner. The outward in this case expresses what is within.

order.why: Ask what is lost when the lamp’s form obscures its light.
Consider the reported contrast between bodily appearance and spiritual recognition.
shortened: As they were looking at his body, they failed to see the light shining within it. But those who looked to the spiritual and the real existence of the Spirit in Christ, firmly believed in him. We must not look at the lantern but at the light--the candle inside.

What made Satan disbelieve in Adam and not worship him? It was only the outward condition of Adam which deterred Satan from believing in him. He would have worshipped him if he had looked at the Spirit in Adam.

order.why: Read the call to look toward an illuminating reality beyond concepts.
Distinguish memorizing a letter from understanding its spirit.
shortened: Thus the Jews thought and spoke, for they did not understand the Scriptures nor the glorious truths that were contained in them. The letter they knew by heart, but of the life-giving spirit they understood not a word.

order.why: Keep the reported generalization about Jewish recognition attributed, without adopting collective blame.
Retain the brief reported statement about failure to understand.
Read the theological claim of scriptural harmony while retaining its polemical voice as attributed.
Consider renewal and the recognition of successive prophets.
Read the hidden mystery through the source’s account of discernment.
Consider the contrast between seeking understanding and seeking superiority.
Hear the image of failing to recognize the rose and its song.
Retain the observation about changed uses of human words.
Pause with the invitation to pass from appearance to inner reality.
shortened: O My handmaid, pass beyond that which is apparent and turn thy gaze towards the inner reality.

order.why: Read understanding as an ocean toward which one strives.
shortened: Strive that perchance through divine assistance ye may attain unto the ocean of inner meanings.

order.why: Begin the sequence on names as barriers to meaning.
Consider recognition that passes beyond the title of successor or mirror.
Examine how even words and deeds can become veils.
shortened: Say: O friends, until ye pass beyond the rivers of names ye shall not attain to the ocean of meanings. Strive that words may not become a barrier and that deeds and utterances may not turn into veils.

order.why: Retain the related invitation to pass beyond names.
shortened: Say: O people! Know with clear certainty that until ye pass beyond the river of names, ye shall not attain unto the ocean of meanings. This is a word that was hidden in the treasuries of My Most Exalted Pen, and We have revealed it in truth and sent it forth with justice.

order.why: Connect this movement with the freedom of the heart.
Read the Point in relation to the letters that arise from it.
shortened: And whoso knoweth the Point is enriched above the knowledge of aught else, and in the inmost of the inmost essence, whoso knoweth the Point knoweth that whereof the outer letters are composed and that which brancheth forth from them.

order.why: Consider the reported image of human lives as creative letters.
Read a hidden outward life through its inward radiance.
Distinguish physical hearing from receptivity without diminishing the person addressed.
Acknowledge that appearance and inward reality can differ.
shortened: There are many souls whose inner reality differs from their outer appearance.

order.why: Read the reported warning that refinement can conceal harmful intentions.
Consider the contrast of outward fire and inward light.
shortened: Though their outer appearance may manifest as fire, their inner reality betokens light. The realm of words does not prevent them from the lofty stations of meaning, nor do metaphorical veils conceal them from the places of truth.

order.why: Read that contrast within the experience of oppression.
shortened: Say: Though the outward appearance of My oppression be as fire, yet its inner reality is light.

order.why: Retain the prayerful image of bitterness and inward sweetness.
Connect inward presence with conduct faithful to divine instruction.
shortened: This pertains to the outward realm; in the inward realm, whosoever hath acted according to the divine commandments and held fast to the Most Holy Book which hath been sent down from the holy Kingdom, is reckoned before God as one of the people of the divine presence.

order.why: Seek correspondence between outward form and inward meaning.
Read the station where inner and outer agree.
Describes outer, inner and further meanings of the divine verses.
Consider the joining of both aspects as an attainment of good.
Hear the hope of seeing through both outward and inward vision.
shortened: Praise be to God Who hath wafted the holy breezes from the divine paradise of meaning upon all created things, that all might behold with both outward and inward vision the lights of the Divine Beauty, and that none upon earth might be prevented or held back from the remembrance of the True Object of Worship.

order.why: Read divine assistance across every degree of inner and outer.
shortened: He is the Protector, He is the Helper, and He is the Succourer of the inner and the outer, and the outer of the outer and the inner of the inner unto whatsoever God willeth.

order.why: Close the linked readings with a blessing upon the whole person.
shortened: May the Glory of God rest upon you, upon the origin of your beings and the end thereof, and upon your outer temples and inner selves.

order.why: Retain the alternate supplied translation and its full reference.
Read the supplied scholar’s account of levels and structure as commentary.
End by returning to the practical test of interpreting a clear instruction.

questions: How can a reader remain open to deeper meaning while respecting a text’s plain instruction?
What helps distinguish a fruitful interpretation from one that merely reflects personal preference?
How do the examples of bread, wine, heaven, and sovereignty illuminate different uses of symbolic language?
What does the explanation of the sower in Mark 4:13–20 suggest about hearing, receiving, and bringing forth fruit?
How might names, labels, or familiarity with words obstruct recognition of their purpose?
What would greater agreement between outward conduct and inward understanding look like in ordinary life?

references.label: 1 · Mark 4:13–20 · The sower and the response to the word
references.note: In the King James Version, Jesus explains the sower’s imagery in terms of hearing, receiving, obstacles, and fruitfulness. Compare this interpretation within the Gospel with the compilation’s concern for moving from verbal familiarity toward understanding and action. An example of symbolic interpretation does not by itself establish that every scriptural instruction should be read symbolically.

subjects.displayTitle: Petitions: making suffering heard and seeking justice
subjects.introduction: Fifty days in a ruined barracks, bad water and worse air, three deaths without a physician, and still no one has named the crime or held an inquiry: so Bahá’u’lláh describes His arrival in ‘Akká in a letter to an official, asking only that the ordinary laws of the state be applied to His followers as to anyone else. A petition makes visible a suffering that power would rather not see, and it must do so without surrendering dignity or courtesy. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells a correspondent to approach the government in a moderate manner, not adversarially; the Báb asks that forged documents be examined and the suspected persons summoned before the ruler’s own eyes. The same movement of asking turns toward God, in prayers for protection from sun and rain, for the uniting of hearts, for forgiveness, and for the strength to serve in the face of opposition. The Book of Acts records a Roman expectation that an accused person should meet the accusers and answer them, a concern for fair hearing these appeals share [1]. From here the way opens toward Bahá’u’lláh’s proclamation to the kings and rulers of the earth, and toward the manner and sweep of the revelation in which such appeals were voiced.
subjects.arc: Begin with the claim to fair treatment, examine the making and reception of appeals, and place practical action beside prayer and inward responsibility.

order.why: Open with the duty to protect an oppressed people through ordinary standards of justice.
shortened: It is, therefore, incumbent on me to present the plea of these oppressed ones before the King of the World. I pray he may show such grace that men will behave towards these downtrodden ones as they do towards others and may not transgress the basic laws of the nations. It befits the sun to rise up and shed its light, and it behoves the cloud to pour down rain. It is, therefore, necessary for his highness the King to look after the interests of an oppressed people.

order.why: Read moderation and fellowship alongside a request for preventive action.
shortened: Thou didst write concerning the disturbances in Bakú. Do thou have recourse to the government so that preventive measures may be taken; yet not in any adversarial fashion: rather, in a moderate manner state thou that such is contrary to justice and inimical to fellowship and love among all the subjects of the respected state.

order.why: Consider investigation of evidence before judgment.
Keep the reported request for a hearing and examination of proofs clearly attributed.
Read the detailed account of confinement, illness, and the absence of inquiry.
shortened: No sooner had we arrived in Acre than they imprisoned us in a ruined barracks, even the women and six-month old children, and they forthwith shut the doors of entry and exit. We have now been imprisoned in the ruined barracks for fifty days, and, on account of the badness of the water and air, we have all been stricken by serious illnesses, such that, after two days, three people died without a physician or food or medicine. Up until now, we have not learnt the nature of our crime. There has been no enquiry. But neither wrongdoing nor acts contrary to the laws have ever been witnessed from us.
We beseech your excellency to turn your attention towards us, so that the breezes of the grace and bounty of his imperial highness the Sultan may blow upon us.

order.why: Hear the concise protest voiced in the name of God and humanity.
shortened: In the name of God and humanity we protest to you against the plight which we have been subjected to from the Turkish government.

order.why: Distinguish a petition for others’ protection from a concern for oneself.
shortened: Since your excellency is informed as to how things are in Iran, I beg of you to present my petition before the throne of the King of the Age, that perchance he may perform an act of grace whereby the hearts of some people may be put at rest, that all may find ease in the cradle of the protection and security of the Monarch of the World and in the shadow of his bounty. The one God is witness that I have not entertained and do not entertain any thought of myself.
But since a large number of individuals have been oppressed, I have felt it necessary to explain how matters stand.

order.why: Read the plea for security and rest under a sovereign’s protection.
shortened: The plea of these servants is that they be shown a merciful glance, so that all may dwell secure and at rest under the protective shadow of the sovereign.

order.why: Consider the Bab’s request that distress and oppression be removed.
shortened: I have risen to mention something of my distress, that by God's will and power it may become the cause of removing oppression.
What is expected from your honor's kindness is that you will, with a glance of favor, arrange for the matter to be resolved in such a way that it is lifted from the source of the decree.

order.why: Read intercession for a poor and sorrowful person.
shortened: Therefore, I hastened to you and came as a delegate before you and appeared in your presence so that you might be the sole intermediary and proper means before a certain person for a poor, sorrowful man - that he might include him within the glances of his eye of care and take him under his protection and guardianship.

order.why: Consider a recommendation offered for someone imprisoned.
Hear the reported appeal against the execution of people described as innocent.
shortened: I have seen a letter in his own handwriting addressed to Fath-'Ali Shah. Once, when the Shah had seized two hundred Turkomans in order to put them to death, Mirza Abu'l-Qasim wrote to the Shah, saying that they were guiltless and did not deserve to be killed.

order.why: Keep the reported call for equal rights and a constitution in its historical setting.
Read the counsel concerning collective complaint within its circumstances.
shortened: Sending a petition directly and individually to the center of government is contrary to wisdom. However, whenever oppression, tyranny and cruelty occur, it is permissible to collectively present the situation and make complaints.

order.why: Consider the requirement that each signatory personally sign.
shortened: Let there be two copies of this petition and the more the believers sign each of these two copies, the better it is. Each person must sign personally. Then (when they are finished) you must forward them here. We will write them the address and forward to that destination.

order.why: Follow the specified stages of appeal in this historical instruction.
shortened: If they harass you again, write the details to Ibrahim Bey, the interpreter at the embassy, and petition His Excellency the Ambassador. If you receive no redress, write directly to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and submit a petition to His Imperial Majesty stating: "We follow the Baha'i religion and have committed no wrong.

order.why: Keep the particular direction about governmental channels tied to its source and occasion.
shortened: Appeal to no authority except the government of His Imperial Majesty, and voice your complaints only in the imperial presence. Seek justice from His Imperial Majesty the King and take your grievances to the respected Prime Minister.

references.note: The King James Version records the expectation that an accused person encounter the accusers and be allowed to answer the charge before being delivered to death. Compare that concern with the requests here for inquiry, examination of documents, and a hearing. The passage belongs to its own narrative and political setting; the comparison concerns fair hearing rather than treating ancient procedure as present legal guidance.
